body_text:
Lagrange's Theorem. If $G$ is a finite group and $H \leq G$ is a
subgroup, then the order $|H|$ divides the order $|G|$, and
$|G| = [G : H] \cdot |H|$, where the index $[G : H]$ is the number
of distinct left cosets of $H$ in $G$.

*Proof Sketch*: Define a relation on $G$ by
$a \sim b \iff a^{-1} * b \in H$. This is an equivalence relation
whose equivalence classes are the left cosets
$aH = \{a * h : h \in H\}$. Left cancellation implies that the map
$h \mapsto a * h$ is a bijection from $H$ onto $aH$, so each coset
contains precisely $|H|$ elements. Since the equivalence classes
partition $G$ into $[G : H]$ disjoint subsets each of size $|H|$,
we conclude $|G| = [G : H] \cdot |H|$.

*Corollaries*:
1. The order of every element $g \in G$ divides $|G|$, since the
   cyclic subgroup $\langle g \rangle$ has order equal to the
   order of $g$. Consequently, $g^{|G|} = e$ for every $g \in G$.
2. (Euler-Fermat): In number theory, applying this to the unit
   group $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$ of order $\varphi(n)$
   yields $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ for all
   $\gcd(a, n) = 1$.
3. Any group of prime order $p$ is cyclic and simple, with no
   non-trivial subgroups.

*Remark*: The converse of Lagrange's theorem is false: if $d$
divides $|G|$, $G$ need not have a subgroup of order $d$. The
alternating group $A_4$ has order $12$, but possesses no subgroup
of order $6$.
